The tundra in North America is richer in both mammals and birds west of Hudson Bay than it is eastward, and richest in Alaska. The most abundant mammals on the tundra are lemmings, and in peak years their numbers are enormous. Among the larger animals, the caribou form large herds and are important in the food and economics of Eskimos and Indians.
A number of birds may be associated with the tundra, particularly during
breeding. Less than one-third of these birds are entirely terrestrial in their life requirements. Many species get their food from the fresh water ponds and lakes or on the margins of these bodies of water, so characteristic of at least the low arctic tundra. Reptiles and amphibians are poorly represented where not absent. Since lakes and ponds and, to an extent, rivers, thaw out for only a few weeks a year, annual production is low. Fish are more numerous in rivers, and are largely migratory salmonids.

Grassland Biome: Grassland presently occurs on all the continents, and at one time covered 42 percent of the earth's surface. Grasslands everywhere possess marked similarities in points of climate, physiognomy, and animal mores. In Russia this community is termed the steppe, in Hungary, the puszta, in South Africa, the veld, and in South America, the pampas.
